title: Chapter 2: Walking the Beaten Path Together 3
content: There were simply too many people, and the space was too small.
So, even if I had overdone it a bit during my first experience, it probably wouldn’t be something to be criticized.
It shouldn’t be, but I couldn’t just let it go unmentioned.
I let out a sigh inwardly.
“Erika, um…”
Her previously satisfied expression turned into one of confusion at my halting words, and it was adorable.
“It’s hard to say…”
“What is it?”
Ah, it really was hard to say.
“The quest… was a failure.”
Upon hearing my words that the quest was a failure, Erika showed a blank expression for a moment, then for some reason, she lowered her face slightly and became bashful.
Her unexpected reaction left me flustered; she was just too cute.
“Um, well, yes, I realize I got a bit carried away.”
She said, glancing at me shyly.
“I understand that in such cases, a lady should show some consideration for the gentlemen, but I just got caught up in the excitement…”
Our eyes met.
“I’m sorry, I got so caught up in the fun that I forgot to leave some for you.”
Erika bowed her head.
“No, it’s not that I’m saying there’s nothing left for me or anything like that.”
“Is that so?”
“Monster hunting isn’t the same as noble hunting.”
Certainly, with her skills, taking down a hundred Bonbo wouldn’t be much different from the deer hunting nobles do for leisure.
Erika murmured, “Ah,” and clapped her hands together.
“Should I have defeated them with my sword?”
“It’s not even about how to defeat them.”
Why would it become a question of how to defeat them?
“I wanted to see if you had the resolve to take a life with your own hands.”
Her thoughts were so battle-oriented, like a warrior. It felt like she had a constant battlefield mentality. I shook my head and told her that wasn’t the case.
“I should have explained better, it’s my fault, but honestly, I underestimated your abilities.”
I bowed my head.
“I didn’t think you could cast that many spells so accurately on multiple moving targets at the same time and in succession. If I had known, I would have explained it beforehand. I’m really sorry.”
Erika showed a puzzled expression at my apology. She probably didn’t yet understand why the quest had failed. To her, the monsters they were supposed to subjugate were already turned to ash.
“I’ll explain, Erika. About the work of an adventurer.”
I gestured for her to follow me as I walked back to where the Bonbo had been.
A beautiful circle of charred grass lay in the grassland.
Given the size of the circle, there must have been two or three Bonbo here.
There were no corpses left, only a small amount of ash remained.
Honestly, I thought there would be a bit more left, but the power displayed was unexpected.
Rather, it clearly showed how extraordinary Erika was, being able to do this to multiple targets at once.
If the royal family and high nobles wanted to keep her away from the academy, they should have graduated her early as an exception instead of trying to eliminate her.
The purpose of establishing the academy was to train individuals who could compete with adventurers.
Her abilities were already at this level after three years; no one would have complained if she graduated.
I marveled at the ridiculous power of the magic and the astonishing precision that ensured it didn’t affect the area outside the circle.
“What do you see?”
Erika tilted her head at my question.
“Just ash.”
“Right, only ash.”
Even someone called a genius like her wouldn’t know, having lived only as a noble. In fact, her fighting style would likely be praised among nobles.
But as an adventurer, it was a problem.
“Do you remember what happens when a monster dies?”
[img]https://i.imgur.com/Y9EVuVW.jpeg
“Magic stones and magic stone fragments, and sometimes a part of its body remains as magic stone fragments,” she answered, somewhat perplexed by the intent of my question.
“Exactly, and we adventurers use those magic stones to prove we’ve defeated the monsters.”
As I said this, Erika quickly realized.
“So, that means… I see, indeed, this would mean the quest is a failure.”
“I’m sorry; I should have explained this from the start. It’s my fault.”
I apologized to Erika, not because I wanted her to feel better, but because it was the right thing to do as an adventurer. Sharing information and understanding is fundamental for adventurers.
This time, I had neglected that, and if my mentor found out, I would get an earful.
“But the real problem isn’t that the quest failed.”
To be blunt, our lives as adventurers were merely a cover, so failing a quest wasn’t particularly troublesome.
However, there were definitely people who would be affected by this failure.
“It means we defeated the monsters, but we can’t show any proof of that to the client.”
The villagers who had requested this quest would be faced with an inconvenient dilemma.
Would they believe the adventurers who claimed they had defeated the monsters but had no way to prove it?

If even one or two magic stones had been left, the situation might have been different, but everything had turned to ash. The fact that even the magic stones of the Bonbo turned to ash in an instant was absurdly powerful.
Continuing to request quests from the Adventurer Guild also incurs costs, and even if they believed we had defeated the monsters, there would still be lingering doubts.
After my explanation, Erika thought for a moment and said, “Let’s take responsibility.”
Erika said she would take responsibility.
Since we had failed, she felt it was her duty to explain.
I told her that explaining through the Adventurer Guild would suffice, but Erika insisted on explaining it herself to the villagers.
That was very much like her.
The farm village was located just a short run from the grassland where we had defeated the Bonbo, thanks to her body enhancement magic.
Even though it was a farm village that supported Hekatai’s food supply, it was well-maintained and quite large.
While there were no barrier devices, it was surrounded by a fence, and magic tools to ward off monsters were set up everywhere. By the way, they looked like scarecrows.
At the village entrance, we released our body enhancement magic, and the elderly guards, who had been waiting with spears at the ready, called out to us as we approached.
“We’re adventurers from Hekatai, here regarding the quest we submitted to the guild. Could you take us to the person in charge?”
I said this while showing my guild badge.
The man looked back and forth between Erika’s and my guild badges with a suspicious expression.
Well, both of us were Rank 1 right now, so I could understand his feelings. Two Rank 1 adventurers showing up, what could they want?
Despite his suspicion, the man seemed to trust our guild badges and allowed us into the village, directing us to the village chief’s house.
Now, what would happen?
“Are you asking me to believe that?”
The village chief’s reaction was not good from the start.
Erika’s explanation was concise and easy to understand, but that was precisely why it was problematic.
It was unreasonable to expect someone to believe that two Rank 1 adventurers had accidentally turned a hundred Bonbo into ash without holding back.
The clarity and simplicity of her explanation only made it sound more absurd.
And to add to that, Erika’s attire was also a problem.
She was dressed quite normally.
An adventurer in a skirt without even any armor was not something you’d typically see.
While she intended to gather proper adventurer gear later, she had chosen a plain outfit with minimal decorations from what she had brought.
In other words, she was wearing clothes that looked like they belonged to a well-off young lady, with a sword belt wrapped around her waist, creating a mismatched appearance.
For me, knowing her abilities, I was confident it wouldn’t be a problem, but to someone who didn’t know her, she would just look like a street girl who had gone a bit overboard.
By the way, I had been mistaken for a guard when I first met Erika, so I understood that.
“There’s no way I can believe that a Rank 1 adventurer turned a horde of Bonbo to ashes without a trace.”
The sun-tanned, square-faced village chief said with a serious expression.
“Well, I figured that would be the case.”
I spoke lightly, knowing it would go this way. It was unforgivable for him not to see Erika’s true abilities, but as the village leader, his words were understandable.
“However, Shin, if this continues, we will unnecessarily burden the villagers.”
I didn’t say it was my fault.
Even if I had, I thought it would only raise more suspicion since the other party didn’t believe us.
“The decision to believe or not lies with the person in charge, not with us.”
Right? I asked the village chief with just my gaze.
He ignored my question, but his eyes, filled with a strong sense of responsibility, told me the answer.
“However…”
Then, another person with a similarly responsible look muttered as if deep in thought.
“However, it is our job to make the person in charge believe us.”
She seemed to be asking with her gaze, but I quickly realized that she had no intention of changing her mind.
There was no way Erika would overlook the fact that someone might suffer due to her failure.
As I nodded, thinking, “This is Erika,” the village chief said with an exasperated tone.
“No matter what you say, I won’t change my judgment.”
“Rest assured.”
Erika smiled.
“I’m an adventurer, after all. I’ll persuade them according to the ways of adventurers.”
With eyes that shone with a strong light, which had once scattered countless noble sons trying to approach the Light Priestess, Erika said this.
There was no such thing as a way of adventurers that Erika spoke of. She said it with such confidence that even I almost believed it.
Naturally, the village chief simply took her words at face value.
Perhaps he thought there was no disadvantage in believing her.
“It’s cramped.”
“Yeah, it is cramped.”
Erika dutifully replied to my muttering.
We were in a shabby little hut on the edge of the village. It was also used for storing farming tools.
After that, Erika had negotiated with the village chief.
She asked if we could stay in the village for a few days until they felt safe.

I thought they might not welcome outsiders staying in their village, but since it was a satellite village of a large city, they seemed accustomed to outsiders, and since it wouldn’t cause any particular disadvantage to the village, they accepted the proposal.
This shabby little hut was what Erika had secured for us to stay in for a few days. Well, it was better than sleeping in an empty house or an inn, as the floor was wooden instead of dirt.
“Well then.”

I placed the blanket I borrowed from the village chief’s kindness to the side so it wouldn’t be in the way and quickly thought about what we needed to do next. Since we had chosen a quest we thought we could complete in a day, I hadn’t prepared at all for an overnight stay. We had secured a place to sleep, but there were still various preparations needed.
First, we needed to secure food and prepare for tomorrow.
“Well then, I’ll go prepare for tomorrow.”
As I said this, Erika tilted her head adorably.
I went out of the shabby hut to prepare for tomorrow, and when I returned, the sun was already quite low in the sky.
“I’m back.”
Erika, who had been cleaning her sword, looked at me with a slightly exasperated expression.
I had two large deer slung over my shoulders and five rabbits hanging from my waist. “You really can do anything,” she thought, but then reconsidered, “No, it’s just that I can’t do anything.”
“It’s too much for just the two of us.”
I understood why Shin had hunted the deer and rabbits, but the sight of him carrying the deer on his shoulders and the rabbits from his waist was amusing, so I couldn’t help but say that.
“As a husband, I got a bit too eager to show my capability.”
Shin, smiling shyly, looked like a young hunter who had just married and was trying too hard to impress his wife.
“In that case, as a wife, I’ll go inform the neighbors that we have some to share.”
Saying this, Erika sheathed her sword. She didn’t realize her voice had a hint of pride in it.
Even in the farm village, pigs were raised for food. However, the main purpose was not for their own consumption but to sell in the city for money.
In other words, opportunities to eat meat were precious. Getting it for free was like a small festival.
Even as a daughter of a high noble born and raised in the royal capital, Erika understood this much.
Free meat is delicious.
In essence, it was a form of payment for our stay.
Since Shin had mentioned preparing for tomorrow, it also served as a greeting. It would be better to be the adventurer who gave them meat than a stranger.
But really, he could do anything.
Watching Shin quickly stack stones to build a stove, Erika was impressed. Despite her enthusiasm about becoming an adventurer, she felt she was doing nothing compared to him.
And here she was, failing and ending up in this situation.
It was her own fault for sleeping in a tool shed, but it must be quite a bother for Shin to be dragged into it. She wished he would at least complain once.
“I’m sorry for making you go through this.”
Once she thought that, Erika couldn’t help but say it. It was a thoughtless statement for someone raised in noble society, where even words of gratitude had to be used cautiously.
Was it too direct?
Shin, who was seasoning the deer meat with herbs, looked back at her with a puzzled expression.
“Would you have preferred wild boar over deer?”
“If you could wait for about two hours, I could go hunt one.”
As Shin continued, Erika was momentarily speechless. While there wasn’t much emotion behind his words, she could tell he was serious.

It was strange; she had just apologized, yet it felt like she was asking for more trouble. Moreover, the sun was setting; even someone raised in the royal capital knew you typically didn’t go hunting after dark.
Why was he asking if she preferred wild boar over deer after she had apologized?
Did she somehow imply, “I’m sorry for making you go (hunting) because of my (preferences)?” No, that couldn’t be it. Erika shook her head.
“Ah, no. That’s not it. I meant about my failure during the day.”
Correcting herself only confused her further.
Why was he troubled?
Shin was pondering while skewering the deer meat with a dagger.
In a low voice, he muttered, “What? Erika’s failure?” If it hadn’t been Shin, she would have thought he was insulting her.
“It’s about burning up the magic stones, you know?”
Ah, Erika felt relieved when Shin finally realized his own failure. Normally, he would have thought it a roundabout way to make her explain her failure.
But knowing he was far from being that indirect only raised another concern.
How had he managed to survive in noble society?
“When I first hunted a monster…”
Then, suddenly, the conversation took a turn.
Was he going to accept her apology or share some wisdom about being an adventurer?
Why was Shin talking about when he first hunted a monster? Erika was confused.
“I had a crushed ankle, my left arm was nearly torn off, and I had more broken ribs than unbroken ones.”
“That sounds like a disaster!”
No matter how she looked at it, it was indeed a disaster.
“Well, I was twelve at the time. I had only been an adventurer for three months.”
That was beyond comprehension. It was abnormal for a noble child to experience such things at twelve.
As Erika was left speechless by his story, Shin shrugged as if to say, “How about that? Funny, right?”
What was funny about that?
“Well, everyone has a rough first hunt.”
This was…
Erika couldn’t help but smile. She was simply happy.
“Are you trying to comfort me?”
Whether the story of twelve-year-old Shin with a crushed ankle, a nearly torn-off arm, and more broken ribs than intact ones was comforting was highly questionable.
For some reason, Shin suddenly looked at the deer meat with a flustered expression.
“I’m sorry; I wish I could have said something more thoughtful.”
Whether it was a sign of embarrassment or not, Shin fiddled with his earlobe while sprinkling salt on the deer meat. There was a strange cuteness about him.
“My father used to say that it’s more enjoyable for a couple to be able to laugh about their failures together.”
I see, Erika thought, impressed.
Like father, like son. It was a rather un-noble way of thinking about enjoying life as a couple. It gave her a glimpse into Shin’s upbringing, and she felt a sense of joy.
That said…
Erika realized she had been feeling down. It was a rather cash-based realization. It was only after being comforted that she noticed her own feelings of melancholy.
She felt like she was relying too much on Shin.
Erika, who tended to be a bit too hard on herself, thought this. She had been prepared for some scolding or complaints. Instead, what she got was Shin’s so-called failure story.
“You’re such a sweet person.”
The words slipped out before she could stop them, and Shin tilted his head, asking, “Are you adding more salt?”
She thought she would apologize again later, but for now—
Erika laughed out loud.
I was satisfied with how things had gone as I spread the blanket on the floor of the shabby hut.
It seemed that the universal way for adventurers to quickly get along with the locals was to treat them to a meal, as my deer and rabbit meat were well received.

It was a village near a large city. I thought meat might not be enough since it was a relatively wealthy farm village, but I was glad it worked out. This would make our work starting tomorrow a bit easier.
We fell asleep, preparing for the next day.
Still, what was it? Even though I was sleeping in the same room as the person I liked, why was I not feeling nervous at all?
I questioned myself as I had grown accustomed to sleeping in the same room during our recent travels, while my mind was busy planning for the next day.
Then, from the darkness, Erika called out to me.
“I apologize, Shin.”
In the darkness, her voice startled me.
“What for?”
I tried to ask calmly, making an effort not to reveal my surprise.
For some reason, I felt that Erika was about to say something, so her sudden apology made me find humor in the fact that we both assumed the other wasn’t asleep.
Was this a continuation of our dinner conversation? I reflexively thought to tell her it was unnecessary to worry about it, but I bit my tongue.
“It’s because of my selfishness that I’m causing you inconvenience.”
“Causing you inconvenience,” huh? I see, it’s not “I’m imposing on you.”
Well, that’s fine.
“Well… that’s true, I can’t deny it.”
For a moment, I thought about denying it, but facts are facts. I wondered if I could become a popular guy if I said something kind here, but my adventurer self got in the way.
Besides, she said “causing,” not “imposing.” If she was imposing something on me, I would be more than willing to accept it.
Perhaps sensing my momentary hesitation, Erika seemed to smile wryly.
“But I don’t dislike it.”
I pushed aside my thoughts about tomorrow’s plans and said this.
“I don’t dislike that sense of responsibility.”
I felt a bit pathetic for saying I didn’t dislike it instead of saying I liked it.
To cover up my embarrassment, I recalled something.
“Besides, I’m used to this kind of thing because of my little sister disciple.”
In fact, considering the degree of trouble, it was quite light.
My little sister disciple, Eluza, was honestly a handful, so the trouble she caused was also quite a handful.
“‘Skewered Eluza,’ was it? I’d love to hear more about that.”
Erika’s casual remark made me chuckle.
“Are you mocking me?”
Her not-so-serious anger felt pleasant.
“I just think it’s blissful not to know.”
If I hadn’t been Shin, I would have thought she was insulting me.
“I want to know even more now.”
I promised myself that I would share that story with her someday soon as I fell asleep.
The next morning, we prepared for the day while being surprised by the villagers who came to fetch tools early.
Preparation meant just using purification magic to clean off the dirt.
By the way, purification magic sounds like an impressive spell.
It’s commonly referred to as a life magic, and it’s widely used by the general public.
To what extent is it common? Even a five-year-old child can use it.
It’s a spell that simply cleans dirt from your body or clothes, but thanks to this magic, we can stay clean anywhere, so I can only be grateful to the ancient sages.
